title: Water at the pump
hookLine: water on one hand, the word spelled into the other, and Helen Keller's locked world opens (The Story of My Life, 4)

lines: A BROKEN DOLL BY THE HEARTH.
DOWN THE PATH TO THE PUMP.
cards: A broken doll lies on the floor by the hearth. The girl who smashed it feels nothing about it, she later writes: no sorrow, no regret.

She can't see and she can't hear, and her teacher has been spelling words into her hand day after day, letters pressed into the palm with quick fingers. The girl can copy the shapes. She has no idea they mean anything.
So her teacher takes her out into the warm day, down the path to the well house, where someone is drawing water at the pump.

teach.h: WATER ON ONE HAND, A WORD IN THE OTHER.
teach.b: First, the two hands. This is Helen Keller's own account, in chapter four of The Story of My Life. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, puts one of Helen's hands under the spout.
Cool water rushes over it. Into the other hand she spells w-a-t-e-r, slowly at first, then fast. Helen stands still, all her attention on those moving fingers.

Something like a forgotten memory stirs, she writes, and the mystery of language comes open. In her words: "I knew then that 'w-a-t-e-r' meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand."
Not a shape in the palm: a name for a thing. And if this had a name, everything did.
Third, the doll. On the way back to the house, she writes, every object she touched seemed alive.

She remembers the doll she broke, feels her way to the hearth, picks up the pieces, and tries, uselessly, to put them together. Now her eyes filled with tears. She understood what she had done, and she was sorry.
A word for water, and then a word for wrong. Fourth, why it's here, in a block on suffering. Her account doesn't say the dark and the silence went away.
They didn't. What changed was that she was no longer alone inside them. Someone had reached in with a name, and a word became a bridge between two people.
She calls it a living word, one that set her soul free.

teach.h: NOT A CURE. A WAY THROUGH.

how: Readers come back to Helen Keller's account of the well house when they think about language, teaching and breakthrough, and the scene is retold in schools and on stage.

o: a deaf-blind girl who found language in a word for water
a blind hymn writer whose songs comforted many
the teacher who spelled words into a child's palm

after the pump, she went back to the doll she had broken
she tried to put the pieces together, and her eyes filled with tears.
Keller writes that the word took away her blindness and deafness
nothing about her senses changed; what changed was that language reached her.

games.q: you're Anne Sullivan. day after day you've spelled words into Helen's hand, and she copies the shapes without understanding. what do you try?
o: spell the same words faster, indoors.
take her to the pump: water on one hand, the word in the other.
games.why: at the well house the cool water and the spelled word meet, and Helen understands that everything has a name.

practice: If you have water near you, let it touch your hand, a few drops on the palm or your fingers around a cold glass; if not, remember the last time water ran over your hands.
Feel only that, cool, wet, moving or still, then slowly trace the letters on your palm with a finger of the other hand: w, a, t, e, r. Feel the thing and its name meet.

wordCard.voice: Helen Keller, blind and deaf, who felt water poured over one hand while her teacher spelled its name into the other, and the world opened. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: water. A word reached her, and she wasn't alone in the dark. Day seven hundred thirty-four, done.
